title: Policy and Legislative Analysis through an Equity Lens
before: Explore how DSD staff examine policies, bills, and recommendations with equity and inclusion built into the work.

turns.text: When you see the title, Policy and Legislative Analysis through an Equity Lens, what work should come to mind? At the Disability Services Division, a policy can shape which services people can use, how resources are distributed, and what staff and partners are expected to do. Policy analysis means understanding the problem, comparing possible responses, and explaining the consequences of a recommendation.

And legislative analysis brings that work to proposed changes in law. Bill analysis gets specific: which provisions change, who has responsibilities, what funding and timing matter, and what an amendment changes. Reading the words carefully matters because a requirement that looks straightforward on paper can have very different effects in people's lives.

So where does equity enter that analysis? From the beginning. Whose experience led us to call something a problem? Who can benefit from the proposed response, and who might still struggle to use it? Those questions shape the options we compare and the recommendation we write. They belong in the substance of the work.

Waiver Reimagine gives us a real Minnesota example. In 2026, the Legislature added advance planning information and a phased transition to the waiver changes. In this course, you'll read the relevant provision and compare it with DHS's published explanation. You'll distinguish what the law directs from what has actually happened in implementation.

Then the practical question becomes: how would someone use that planning information to make decisions about their support? They may need time to understand it, discuss their choices, and get answers. An analyst can examine whether the approach supports that purpose, including for people facing language, disability, geographic, or other barriers.

That takes more than one perspective. Legislative colleagues explain the proposal and its implications. Program staff understand service arrangements. Fiscal colleagues examine costs and assumptions. The equity consultant helps investigate barriers and compare responses. Staff with different responsibilities and experiences need a meaningful opportunity to challenge an assumption, including when they are newer to the team.

And people receiving services bring knowledge that an internal team cannot supply for them. If their experience changes our understanding of a proposal, it should change the analysis. We'll also look at DHS's intervention and respite service redesign, where published community feedback raises questions about how services work together. What would you change in a recommendation after hearing that?

That's a question you'll practice. You'll consider whose perspective is missing, what the evidence supports, and which options respond to the concern. A culture brief can help you prepare thoughtful questions. It cannot tell you what every person in a community wants, or replace asking people directly while there is still something they can influence.

We'll connect this to resources, too. A fiscal note estimates a bill's financial effects. Equity analysis asks additional questions about how benefits and burdens are distributed. An approach may save staff time but require more unpaid effort from families. Understanding both helps us compare options honestly and explain what support implementation would need.

By the end, you'll have practiced reading a provision, weighing community and staff knowledge, comparing alternatives, and writing a concise recommendation. You'll also revisit a conclusion when the underlying text changes. Whether you analyze legislation, advise leadership, work with service partners, or estimate costs, you'll have a concrete way to contribute your knowledge to a stronger analysis.

Keep a decision from your own work in mind as you go. What would you want a colleague to explain before you could support it? The aim here is to help you make that explanation clear: what could change, for whom, why you recommend it, and what you still need to understand.

guidance.title: When barriers overlap
guidance.text: A person may need an accessible explanation and support in their preferred language. Providing one without the other may still leave important choices unclear. Intersectionality helps us examine how those conditions work together. Start with the person’s experience. Which parts of the policy or service make it harder to act on the information, and what would help?

guidance.title: Let the evidence change your recommendation
guidance.text: You may already have an approach you prefer. That is a useful place to begin. Before you settle on it, consider what a person using the service or a colleague carrying out the change might notice. If their experience changes your recommendation, that is the analysis doing its job. What would you want to ask them?
